title: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
summary: How Megatron Core splits LLM training over thousands of GPUs: tensor, pipeline, sequence and context parallelism, the distributed optimizer, and how to measure the result with MFU.
outcomes: Explain why Megatron splits the MLP column-wise then row-wise and compute TP traffic per layer as 8bsh(t-1)/t
Compute the pipeline bubble (p-1)/(vm) and explain what 1F1B and interleaving each fix
Compute per-layer activation memory with TP, sequence parallelism and selective recompute
Compute MFU from tokens per second and tell it apart from hardware FLOPs utilization
Choose TP, PP, CP and DP sizes for a cluster and justify which link each one uses

lessons.title: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it

blocks.md:
Recall a training step from the prerequisites: a forward pass computes the loss, a backward pass computes a gradient for every weight, and the optimizer (usually Adam) updates the weights. Every step must keep the weights, their gradients and the optimizer state in GPU memory, plus the *activations*: tensors saved during the forward pass because the backward pass needs them.

Megatron Core (MCore) is NVIDIA's library, in the [NVIDIA/Megatron-LM](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM) repo, of GPU-optimized transformer building blocks and parallelism strategies for spreading this work over thousands of GPUs. This course explains each strategy, the formulas that predict its cost, and how to measure the result.

Start with memory. The Megatron Core distributed optimizer docs count the bytes each parameter needs with BF16 weights and FP32 gradients: 2 (BF16 weight) + 4 (FP32 gradient) + 4 (FP32 *main* copy of the weight that the optimizer updates) + 4 + 4 (Adam's two moment estimates) = **18 bytes per parameter**.

For GPT-3 with 175 billion parameters that is 175e9 x 18 bytes = **3,150 GB**, before a single activation is stored. An A100 or H100 has 80 GB. Even ignoring activations, the model state alone needs at least 40 GPUs worth of memory.

blocks.title: Model state of GPT-3 175B (BF16 weights, FP32 grads, Adam)

scenes.caption: Each FP32 tensor costs 4 bytes x 175e9 = 700 GB; the BF16 weights cost 350 GB. Together 3,150 GB: about 39 times the 80 GB of one GPU.

blocks.md:
Compute is the second wall. Narayanan et al. (2021) estimate that training GPT-3 on a single V100 would take about **288 years**. So we need many GPUs both to *fit* the model and to *finish* in weeks.

*Data parallelism* (DP), which you know from the prerequisites, gives every GPU a full copy of the model and a slice of the batch, then averages gradients with an all-reduce. It solves the time problem only when the model fits on one GPU, and the paper notes two more limits: the per-GPU batch gets too small to keep the GPU busy, and you can never use more GPUs than there are samples in the batch.

Megatron splits the work along five axes. Each one cuts a different dimension of the computation:

- **Tensor parallelism (TP)**: split the weight matrices *inside* each layer across GPUs.
- **Pipeline parallelism (PP)**: give each GPU a contiguous slice of the layers.
- **Data parallelism (DP)**: replicate the (already split) model and split the batch.
- **Context parallelism (CP)**: split the sequence (the tokens of one sample) across GPUs.
- **Expert parallelism (EP)**: in mixture-of-experts models, place different experts on different GPUs.

The combination of the first three is what the 2021 paper calls **PTD-P**.

blocks.title: 8 GPUs as TP=2 x PP=2 x DP=2

scenes.caption: A 24-layer model on 8 GPUs. Each box is a tensor-parallel pair: two GPUs that together hold one copy of 12 layers, each GPU owning half of every weight matrix.
Pipeline parallelism: the first pair runs layers 1-12 and sends its output activations to the pair running layers 13-24. Point-to-point sends, once per microbatch.
Data parallelism: replica B holds the same weights as replica A but sees different samples. After the backward pass, matching shards average their gradients.
Megatron's default rank order is tp-cp-ep-dp-pp: TP varies fastest, so a TP group is consecutive ranks on one server, where the fast NVLink links are.

blocks.caption: The GPU count for the dense (non-expert) layers, as given in the Megatron Core context parallel docs. Mixture-of-experts layers regroup the same GPUs (lesson 5).

blocks.md: Every axis splits something different: TP splits matrices, PP splits layers, DP splits the batch, CP splits the sequence, EP splits experts. Choosing a configuration means choosing which communication you can afford on which link.

blocks.question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
blocks.explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

blocks.question: Why does the 3,150 GB figure for GPT-3 175B not even include the largest memory user in many training runs?
options: It ignores the activations saved for the backward pass, which grow with batch size and sequence length
It ignores the tokenizer vocabulary
It counts Adam moments in BF16 instead of FP32
It forgets the gradients
blocks.explain: 18 bytes per parameter covers weights, gradients, main weights and Adam moments. Activations come on top and scale with microbatch size, sequence length and layer count. Lesson 4 is entirely about them.

lessons.title: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention

blocks.md:
The transformer MLP is two matrix multiplies (GEMMs) with a GeLU in between: $Y = \text{GeLU}(XA)$, then $Z = \text{Dropout}(YB)$. Here $X$ has $h$ features per token, $A$ is $h \times 4h$ and $B$ is $4h \times h$.

Shoeybi et al. (2019) asked: how do we split $A$ and $B$ over $t$ GPUs so that each GPU does $1/t$ of the math and the GPUs talk as little as possible? There are two ways to cut a matrix, by rows or by columns, and the choice matters because GeLU is nonlinear.

blocks.prompt: Option 1: split $A$ by rows (and $X$ by columns), so GPU $i$ computes $X_i A_i$ and the true pre-activation is $X_1A_1 + X_2A_2$. Can each GPU apply GeLU to its own partial result and add afterwards?
blocks.reveal: No. $\text{GeLU}(X_1A_1 + X_2A_2) \neq \text{GeLU}(X_1A_1) + \text{GeLU}(X_2A_2)$. With the numbers in the next figure, the first output feature should be GeLU(1 + 1) = 1.954, but GeLU(1) + GeLU(1) = 1.683. A row split forces a synchronization (summing the partials) *before* the GeLU.

blocks.md:
Option 2: split $A$ by **columns**, $A = [A_1, A_2]$. Now each GPU holds the full input $X$ and computes complete pre-activations for its own half of the $4h$ features, so GeLU applies locally: $[Y_1, Y_2] = [\text{GeLU}(XA_1), \text{GeLU}(XA_2)]$. No communication.

The second GEMM is then split by **rows**, $B = [B_1; B_2]$, so GPU $i$ multiplies the $Y_i$ it already has: $YB = Y_1B_1 + Y_2B_2$. Each GPU now holds a *partial sum* of the output, and one all-reduce (sum across GPUs) produces $Z$.

blocks.title: One token through a 2-way tensor-parallel MLP

scenes.caption: Input token x = [1, 2] is replicated on both GPUs. A is 2 x 4 with columns (1, 0.5), (-1, 1), (0.5, -1), (2, -0.5).
Column split: GPU0 owns A's first two columns, GPU1 the last two. Pre-activations xA = [2, 1, -1.5, 1]; each GPU applies GeLU to its own two features with no communication.
Row split of B, whose rows are (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1), (-1, 0.5): GPU0 multiplies its y1 by the first two rows, GPU1 its y2 by the last two. Each result is a partial sum with the full output width.
The g operator all-reduces the partials: z = [1.013, 1.162] on both GPUs, exactly what one GPU computing the full MLP gets. One all-reduce for the whole MLP.

blocks.md:
Self-attention splits the same way, using the fact that heads are independent. The $Q$, $K$ and $V$ projections are **column-parallel**: each GPU gets whole heads (with $t$-way TP, $a/t$ of the $a$ heads) and runs attention for them locally. The output projection is **row-parallel** and ends in one all-reduce.

So a full transformer layer needs two all-reduces in the forward pass and two in the backward pass. The paper's names for the two communication points are $f$ and $g$:

- $f$ (before the column-parallel GEMM): identity forward, all-reduce of the input gradient backward.
- $g$ (after the row-parallel GEMM): all-reduce forward, identity backward.

blocks.caption: Abridged from megatron/core/tensor_parallel/mappings.py. The paper's f and g really are a few lines of PyTorch autograd.

blocks.md:
Why does $f$ all-reduce in the backward pass? Each GPU used the same $X$ but only its own columns of $A$, so each computes only part of $\partial L/\partial X$; the true gradient is the sum. $g$ mirrors it: summed outputs forward, and the gradient of a sum copies straight through.

The embedding is split too: the input embedding matrix is partitioned along the vocabulary, and the output layer fuses the parallel logits GEMM with the cross-entropy loss so GPUs exchange per-token scalars instead of $b \times s \times v$ logits.

**How much does TP communicate?** Let $b$ be the microbatch size (the number of sequences in one forward pass; lesson 3 explains microbatches), $s$ the sequence length and $h$ the hidden size. Each all-reduce acts on a $b \times s \times h$ tensor, and a ring all-reduce over $t$ GPUs sends about $2(t-1)/t$ times the tensor size per GPU. Four all-reduces per layer (two forward, two backward) give the per-layer, per-microbatch volume from Narayanan et al.:

blocks.tex: V_{\text{TP}} = 8\,bsh\,\frac{t-1}{t} \;\text{elements per layer per GPU} \qquad V_{\text{PP}} = bsh \;\text{per stage boundary per direction}
blocks.caption: Pipeline parallelism, by contrast, sends one bsh activation tensor between neighbouring stages (forward) and one gradient tensor back.

blocks.md:
Worked example, GPT-3 175B ($s = 2048$, $h = 12288$, $b = 1$, BF16 so 2 bytes per element, $t = 8$):

- One all-reduce payload: $bsh$ = 25.2M elements = **50 MB**.
- TP per layer: $8 \cdot bsh \cdot 7/8$ = 176M elements = **352 MB** per microbatch.
- With 96 layers on 8 pipeline stages (12 layers each), every GPU moves about **4.2 GB** of TP traffic per microbatch.
- The pipeline sends 50 MB per stage boundary per direction, and only **6.3 MB** per GPU with the paper's scatter/gather trick (each of the 8 TP ranks sends 1/8 over its own InfiniBand card, then they all-gather over NVLink).

blocks.title: TP traffic vs pipeline traffic per microbatch (units of bsh)

y.label: elements sent per GPU, in units of bsh

scenes.caption: Per layer, TP traffic approaches 8 bsh as t grows; it does not shrink with more GPUs. A 12-layer stage at t = 8 moves 84 bsh per microbatch, versus 2 bsh for the pipeline.
With only 2 layers per stage, TP traffic is still 14 bsh at t = 8. Pipeline sends are point-to-point and small, which is why PP is the axis that crosses slow inter-node links.

blocks.md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

blocks.question: In a 2-way TP MLP, an engineer splits the first weight matrix A by rows instead of columns, keeping everything else the same. What breaks?
options: Nothing, matrix multiplication is linear so the split does not matter
GeLU is applied to partial sums, so outputs are wrong unless an extra all-reduce is inserted before the GeLU
The backward pass needs twice as much memory
The second GEMM can no longer be split
blocks.explain: A row split of A gives each GPU a partial pre-activation. GeLU is nonlinear, so GeLU of the parts does not add up to GeLU of the whole (1.683 vs 1.954 in the example). The column split avoids this synchronization entirely.

blocks.question: For a fixed model, a team doubles TP from 4 to 8 inside a server. Per GPU and per layer, how does TP communication volume change?
options: It halves, because each GPU holds half as many weights
It stays the same
It grows from 6 bsh to 7 bsh, about 17% more
It doubles
blocks.explain: Volume is 8bsh(t-1)/t: 8 x 3/4 = 6 bsh at t = 4 and 8 x 7/8 = 7 bsh at t = 8. Communication does not shrink with more TP ranks while compute per GPU halves, so the communication share of each step rises.

lessons.title: Pipeline parallelism: bubbles, 1F1B and the interleaved schedule

blocks.md:
Pipeline parallelism gives each of $p$ devices a contiguous slice of layers: a *stage*. A single sample would leave all but one stage idle, so the batch is cut into $m$ **microbatches** that flow through the stages one after another, like cars on an assembly line.

Megatron keeps *strict optimizer semantics*: every microbatch's forward and backward pass uses the same weights, and the optimizer steps once at the end of the batch. That requires a **pipeline flush**: all microbatches must drain before the update. Devices idle while the pipeline fills and drains, and this idle time is the **pipeline bubble**.

blocks.title: Three schedules for p = 4 devices and m = 8 microbatches

scenes.caption: GPipe: all forwards (blue, 1 unit) then all backwards (2 units). Simplified: no communication time. The ideal is 8 x 3 = 24 units (marker), but the flush ends at 33.
1F1B (PipeDream-Flush): after a short warm-up, each device alternates one forward and one backward. Still 33 units: the bubble is identical. What changes is memory (next figure).
Interleaved 1F1B with v = 2 chunks per device: device 1 runs stages 1 and 5, device 2 stages 2 and 6, and so on. Each chunk is half the work, so fill and drain shrink: done at 28.5.

blocks.md: Count the bubble in the GPipe picture. Device 4 cannot start until $p-1$ forward passes have happened upstream, and device 1 waits through $p-1$ backward passes at the end. With per-microbatch forward and backward times $t_f$ and $t_b$, the bubble is $(p-1)(t_f + t_b)$, while the useful work is $m(t_f + t_b)$. For the figure: $3 \times 3 = 9$ idle units against 24 ideal, so the flush ends at 33.

blocks.caption: From Narayanan et al. (2021): bubble time divided by ideal time. With v model chunks per device, each chunk's forward and backward take t_f / v and t_b / v, so the fill and drain shrink v times.

blocks.md:
**1F1B fixes memory, not the bubble.** GPipe runs all $m$ forwards before any backward, so every device stashes activations for all $m$ microbatches. In 1F1B, device $d$ (counting from 0) does only $p - d - 1$ warm-up forwards, then strictly alternates one forward and one backward, so a device never holds more than $p$ microbatches in flight. When $m \gg p$ that is a large saving, and it is the schedule Megatron uses.

**Interleaving attacks the bubble.** Instead of device 1 owning layers 1-4 of a 16-layer model, it owns layers 1-2 and 9-10 (two *model chunks*), device 2 owns 3-4 and 11-12, and so on. Megatron calls these *virtual pipeline stages*. The cost: $v$ times more point-to-point sends, and the paper's schedule needs $m$ to be a multiple of $p$ (current Megatron Core relaxes this somewhat).

blocks.title: Peak microbatches of activations held per device

scenes.caption: GPipe: every device stores activations for all 8 microbatches before its first backward pass.
1F1B: device d holds at most p - d microbatches (4, 3, 2, 1). Device 1 holds the most: p microbatches of L/p layers each, a full model's worth of layer activations.
Interleaved (v = 2), measured in full-stage units: 5.5, 4.5, 3.5, 2.5. Device 1 holds 1 + (p-1)/(pv) = 1.375 times the 1F1B amount, matching Korthikanti et al.
p = 4, v = 1: at m = 8 the bubble is 3/8 = 37.5% of ideal time (27% of the whole step). You need m much larger than p.
Interleaving with v = 2 halves it: 3/16 = 18.75% at m = 8, as in the timeline.
p = 8 at m = 32 gives 7/32 = 21.9%; with v = 4 it drops to 5.5%. Deep pipelines need many microbatches or interleaving.

blocks.prompt: The global batch is fixed. A team doubles the microbatch size $b$ to make each GEMM bigger and more efficient. What happens to the bubble?
blocks.reveal: It grows. With global batch $B$ and data-parallel size $d$, the number of microbatches is $m = B/(b \cdot d)$, so doubling $b$ halves $m$ and doubles $(p-1)/m$. Narayanan et al. show the two effects fight: larger microbatches raise per-GPU efficiency (up to 1.3x on one GPU in their Figure 7) but enlarge the bubble, so the best $b$ is model dependent (4 for one model, 2 for their 91B config).

blocks.md: In Megatron, interleaving is set with `--num-layers-per-virtual-pipeline-stage`. The MoE guide notes that the valid values divide num_layers / PP and that larger v means fewer bubbles but more point-to-point traffic, so a middle value is often best.
Bubble = (p - 1) / (v m). 1F1B bounds activation memory to p microbatches; interleaving divides the bubble by v at the cost of v times more pipeline sends.

blocks.question: p = 8 pipeline stages, m = 32 microbatches, interleaved with v = 4 chunks per device. What is the bubble as a fraction of ideal time?
blocks.explain: (p - 1) / (v m) = 7 / (4 x 32) = 7/128 = 5.5%. Without interleaving it would be 7/32 = 21.9%.

blocks.question: Why did Megatron adopt 1F1B (PipeDream-Flush) over GPipe even though both have the same bubble?
options: 1F1B needs no pipeline flush
1F1B sends fewer bytes between stages
1F1B caps in-flight microbatches at p instead of m, so activation memory stops growing with the number of microbatches
1F1B lets each microbatch use slightly stale weights, which is faster
blocks.explain: The bubble is (p-1)/m for both. GPipe stores activations for all m microbatches; 1F1B starts backward passes early and never has more than p outstanding. This is what makes a large m (small bubble) affordable.

lessons.title: Activation memory: sequence parallelism, selective recompute, CP

blocks.md:
After TP and PP split the weights, activations become the memory problem. Korthikanti et al. (2022) count, for one transformer layer in 16-bit, the bytes saved for the backward pass ($a$ = attention heads):

- Attention block: $11sbh + 5as^2b$. The $s^2$ terms are the softmax output, its dropout mask and the dropout output: one $s \times s$ matrix per head.
- MLP: $19sbh$ (inputs of both GEMMs, the GeLU input of width $4h$, a dropout mask).
- Two layer norms: $4sbh$.

blocks.caption: Equation 1 of Korthikanti et al. For GPT-3 (a = 96, s = 2048, h = 12288) 5as/h = 80, so the attention-score term is more than twice the rest.

blocks.md:
Tensor parallelism splits the activations *inside* the attention and MLP blocks, but not the layer norms, the dropouts after each block, or the inputs to the blocks. These are replicated on all $t$ GPUs: $10sbh$ that does not shrink with $t$. Per layer, TP gives $sbh(10 + 24/t + 5as/(ht))$.

**Sequence parallelism (SP)** observes that layer norm and dropout act on each token independently, so those regions can be split along the *sequence* dimension. Each of the $t$ GPUs keeps $s/t$ of the tokens there. The TP all-reduce is replaced by its two halves: an **all-gather** entering the TP region and a **reduce-scatter** leaving it.

blocks.title: One MLP block with TP = 2 plus sequence parallelism

scenes.caption: Sequence-parallel region: each GPU runs layer norm on its own half of the tokens (s/2 x b x h). Nothing is replicated.
Operator g, forward: all-gather along the sequence. Each GPU now has the full Y it needs as input to the column-parallel GEMM.
Tensor-parallel region: GEMM with A's columns, GeLU, GEMM with B's rows, exactly as in lesson 2. Each GPU ends with a partial sum W_i of the full output.
Operator g-bar, forward: reduce-scatter. Partials are summed and each GPU keeps only its own tokens, ready for the sequence-split dropout.
Backward swaps the roles: g-bar becomes an all-gather of gradients and g a reduce-scatter. Every collective has a conjugate.

blocks.md: SP adds no communication volume: a ring all-reduce is literally a reduce-scatter followed by an all-gather, so TP + SP moves the same bytes as TP. It just stops storing replicated activations. Per layer memory becomes sbh(34 + 5as/h) / t: everything divided by t.

**Selective activation recomputation.** The $5as/h$ term comes from attention scores, softmax and its dropout: huge tensors (quadratic in $s$) with very few FLOPs per element. Recomputing *only those* in the backward pass, instead of the whole layer, removes the term at little cost.

For GPT-3 the recomputed part is $4bs^2h$ extra FLOPs per layer (the $QK^T$ and attention-over-$V$ GEMMs). Our script: that is $4s/(24h + 4s)$ = **2.7%** of the forward FLOPs (the paper's figure), or 0.9% of a full forward plus backward step. In exchange it saves $80/114$ = **70%** of the activation memory.

blocks.title: GPT-3 175B: activation memory per layer (t = 8, b = 1)

scenes.caption: One layer on one GPU with no splitting: sbh(34 + 80) = 2.87 GB. Times 96 layers that is 275 GB.
TP = 8 cuts it to 0.58 GB. But the replicated 10 sbh (layer norms, dropouts, block inputs) is 0.25 GB of that, 43% of what is left, and it never shrinks with t.
Adding SP (0.36 GB) or selective recompute (0.33 GB) each nearly halves the TP figure. Together: 34 sbh / t = 0.107 GB, 18.5% of TP alone: the paper's 5x reduction.
Full recompute stores only each layer's input, 2 sbh = 0.050 GB, but reruns the whole forward pass (30 to 40% time overhead in the paper). SP + selective gets within about 2x of it for about 4%.

blocks.md:
Now multiply by layers. With 1F1B, pipeline stage 1 holds $p$ microbatches of $L/p$ layers each, so it stores **$L$ layers worth** of activations regardless of $p$ (lesson 3). For GPT-3 with TP = 8, SP and selective recompute: 96 x 0.107 GB = **10.3 GB** on the first stage; with interleaving ($p = 8$, $v = 3$) multiply by $1 + (p-1)/(pv) = 1.29$ to get **13.3 GB**. With TP alone it would be 55.6 GB; the paper reports that with TP alone and no recompute, every one of its test models (22B to 1T) needs more than the 80 GB of an A100.

Measured on a 22B layer, full recompute added 39% to the layer's forward plus backward time; SP plus selective recompute added 4%.

The 5as/h term assumes attention materializes the s x s score matrix. Fused attention kernels (FlashAttention style, as in Transformer Engine) never store it, so most of that term disappears by itself. Megatron Core's config even warns that with fused attention there is no need to put core_attn in --recompute-modules.

**Context parallelism (CP)** goes further than SP: it splits *all* activations, including attention, along the sequence. Linear layers and norms work per token, so they need no change. Attention does need every key and value, so the Megatron Core docs describe exchanging KV chunks between the GPUs of a CP group in a ring (all-gather forward, reduce-scatter of KV gradients backward), with load balancing for causal masks. The guide recommends CP for sequences of 8K tokens and longer, and suggests it in place of larger TP when long sequences cause out-of-memory errors.

blocks.question: A model has 5as/h = 20 (short sequences, wide hidden size). Compared with GPT-3 (5as/h = 80), how much does selective recompute help it?
options: Exactly as much, it always saves 70%
More: it removes 80% because the model is wider
Nothing, selective recompute only works with sequence parallelism
Less: it removes 20/54 = 37% of activation memory
blocks.explain: Selective recompute removes the 5as/h part of 34 + 5as/h. For 5as/h = 20 that is 20/54 = 37%. The trick shines for long sequences and many heads, where the quadratic attention term dominates.

blocks.question: Why does sequence parallelism not increase communication over plain TP?
options: It compresses activations before sending them
It skips the backward-pass communication
An all-reduce is a reduce-scatter plus an all-gather, and SP issues exactly those two halves at different points
It sends activations only between pipeline stages
blocks.explain: TP does 4 all-reduces per layer per step; TP + SP does 4 all-gathers and 4 reduce-scatters. A ring all-reduce is implemented as reduce-scatter then all-gather, so the bandwidth used is the same. The paper even measured a small speedup from running layer norm and dropout on 1/t of the data.

lessons.title: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU

blocks.md:
Back to the 18 bytes per parameter from lesson 1. Plain DP replicates all of it on every data-parallel rank. Megatron Core's **distributed optimizer** shards the optimizer part across the $d$ data-parallel ranks, as in ZeRO: each rank keeps FP32 main weights and Adam moments for only $1/d$ of the parameters.

The docs give the per-parameter cost (BF16 weights, FP32 gradients) as $6 + 12/d$ bytes: 2 for the weight and 4 for the gradient buffer are kept everywhere, 12 bytes of optimizer state are sharded.

blocks.title: Distributed optimizer step on 4 data-parallel ranks

scenes.caption: Backward pass done: each rank holds local gradients for all 16 elements, computed from its own slice of the batch.
Reduce-scatter: rank 0 now holds the fully summed gradient for elements 0-3, rank 1 for 4-7, and so on. The other 12 slots on each rank are stale.
optimizer.step(): each rank updates only its 4 FP32 main weights (it owns only those Adam moments) and casts them to BF16 parameters.
All-gather: every rank receives the other 12 updated BF16 parameters and can start the next forward pass. Reduce-scatter plus all-gather moves the same number of elements as one gradient all-reduce.

blocks.title: Bytes per parameter vs data-parallel size
blocks.caption: BF16 weights, FP32 gradients. At d = 8 the cost is 7.5 bytes, at d = 64 6.19 bytes: GPT-3's state drops from 3,150 GB to about 1,083 GB per model copy.

scenes.caption: At d = 8 the distributed optimizer needs 7.5 bytes per parameter instead of 18; it approaches 6 as d grows. Megatron-FSDP goes further and also shards gradients and weights (ZeRO-2 and ZeRO-3 style).

blocks.md:
**Overlap.** Communication that runs while the GPU computes is free. Megatron's README lists the flags its benchmarks use: `--overlap-grad-reduce` (start reducing gradients for layers whose backward is done while earlier layers are still in backward), `--overlap-param-gather` (gather the next layers' weights during the forward pass), `--tp-comm-overlap` (hide TP collectives behind GEMMs), and pipeline send/receive overlap, which is on by default.

**Mixture of experts.** Expert parallelism (EP) puts different experts on different GPUs and moves tokens to their experts with all-to-all communication. Megatron Core's *MoE parallel folding* lets attention layers use TP x CP x DP x PP while the MoE layers regroup the same GPUs as ETP x EP x EDP x PP (expert TP, EP, expert DP). For example attention with TP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 8 can run its experts with EP = 64. The MoE guide advises keeping EP x TP inside one NVLink domain.

**Measuring the result.** PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022) defined **model FLOPs utilization (MFU)**: observed tokens per second divided by the tokens per second the hardware could process at peak FLOP/s. Only FLOPs the *model* requires count. A dense decoder with $N$ parameters needs $6N$ matmul FLOPs per token (2N forward, 4N backward), plus $12LHQT$ for attention ($L$ layers, $H$ heads, head size $Q$, sequence length $T$). Recomputation is *not* counted, so MFU cannot be gamed by doing extra work. **Hardware FLOPs utilization (HFU)** counts everything the GPU actually executed, recompute included.

Worked example: the 530B GPT model (105 layers, $h$ = 20480, 128 heads, $s$ = 2048) from Korthikanti et al., on 280 A100s (peak 312 TFLOP/s BF16) with TP = 8, PP = 35, batch 280 sequences, measured at 37.83 s per iteration.

1. Tokens per second: 280 x 2048 / 37.83 = 15,158.
2. $6N$ part: 15,158 x 6 x 529.6e9 / (280 x 312e12) = 55.1%.
3. Attention part: $12 \cdot 105 \cdot 128 \cdot 160 \cdot 2048$ FLOPs per token adds 0.9%.
4. **MFU = 56.0%**, matching the paper. The paper's HFU of 57.0% uses its Equation 8, which counts the recompute generously; adding only the $4bs^2h$ recomputed FLOPs per layer gives about 56.3%. Scaling to 8-way DP (2,240 GPUs, 39.15 s) gives 54.2%.

blocks.title: Same hardware counter, different stories: HFU vs MFU

scenes.caption: Narayanan et al.'s 1T model: 163 TFLOP/s per GPU = 52.2% of 312, counted with full recompute (96 instead of 72 in the FLOP formula). Dropping the recompute FLOPs gives an MFU of about 39.2%.
Korthikanti et al.'s 530B run with SP + selective recompute: HFU 57.0% and MFU 56.0%. Almost no wasted FLOPs, so the two metrics nearly agree, and true speed is far higher.
For comparison PaLM computes the production MT-NLG 530B run (65.43K tokens/s on 2,240 A100s) at about 30.2% MFU, and PaLM 540B at 46.2% MFU with 57.8% HFU.

blocks.md: Do not compare a paper's achieved TFLOP/s across systems without checking what it counts. Narayanan et al.'s 52% includes recomputation FLOPs; PaLM introduced MFU precisely because HFU depends on implementation choices like rematerialization.

Today's reference points from the Megatron-LM README: up to **47% MFU** on H100 clusters, rising from 41% for the smallest benchmarked model to 47 to 48% for the largest because bigger GEMMs are more efficient, and falling from 47% to 42% when strong-scaling GPT-3 175B from 96 to 4,608 GPUs at a fixed batch of 1,152 sequences, as communication becomes exposed.

The Megatron Core guide's order for choosing a configuration: start with DP (plus the distributed optimizer), add TP inside a node if the model does not fit, add PP across nodes for very large models, add CP for long sequences, and use activation recompute or offload only in extreme cases.
Every knob in this course trades three things: memory per GPU, communication on a specific link, and idle or redundant compute. MFU is the single number that tells you whether the trade worked.

blocks.prompt: A run reports 50% 'GPU utilization' using full activation recomputation. Roughly what MFU should you expect, ignoring attention and logits?
blocks.reveal: About 37.5%. Full recompute adds one extra forward pass: per token the hardware does 2N (forward) + 2N (recomputed forward) + 4N (backward) = 8N FLOPs instead of 6N. MFU = HFU x 6/8 = 50% x 0.75 = 37.5%. The 1T example above shows the same 72/96 ratio: 52.2% becomes about 39%.

blocks.question: A Llama-style 70B model is trained with 8K-token sequences on 64 GPUs (8 per node). Which configuration fits the Megatron Core guidance best?
options: TP = 4, PP = 4, CP = 2, DP = 2
TP = 64, nothing else
TP = 1, PP = 64
TP = 16 across two nodes, DP = 4
blocks.explain: This is the guide's own example: TP stays inside a node, PP splits the 80 layers across nodes, CP = 2 handles the 8K sequence, and DP uses what is left (4 x 4 x 2 x 2 = 64). TP = 64 or 16 crosses nodes with all-reduces every layer; PP = 64 gives a huge bubble.

blocks.question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
blocks.explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.
